samples.summary: CLI auth code is still not bound to the client (no PKCE); the nonce only gates the local listener, so an intercepted code is fully redeemable
samples.evidence: The change cites RFC 8252 §8.9, whose actual prescription for the loopback-redirect code-injection problem is PKCE. What landed is a `state` echo checked only inside the CLI's own listener (`packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:206`). The code itself remains an unbound bearer: `POST /auth/cli/exchange` (auth.controller.ts:152-168) takes `{ code }` with no authentication, no `code_verifier`, and no reference to the nonce — `consumeCode` looks up only the code (cli-auth.store.ts:71). Attack: anyone who observes the code within its 60s TTL — from the victim's browser history/URL bar (`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=…` is a real navigation), a browser extension, a shared/kiosk machine, or an intercepting proxy — POSTs it to /auth/cli/exchange and receives the victim's `accessToken` + `refreshToken`. The nonce does nothing here because the CLI listener is not in the path. Grepped the whole repo for pkce/code_verifier/code_challenge: zero hits. Severity is 'major' rather than 'critical' because it needs code interception, and confidence is low because I could not demonstrate a concrete interception channel in this codebase.

samples.summary: The nonce is optional server-side, so the new anti-injection binding is opt-in and silently absent for any client that omits it
samples.evidence: `createState(mode, portNum, nonce ?? undefined)` accepts `mode=cli` with no nonce at all (github-auth.guard.ts:34-38), and auth.controller.ts:130-132 then emits the redirect with no `state` at all. Nothing in the backend requires a nonce for a CLI flow. Consequence: (a) every already-installed pre-nonce CLI keeps the original RFC 8252 §8.9 code-injection exposure against the same backend, with no server-side signal that the binding is missing; (b) an attacker can deliberately mint nonce-less CLI states. It is fail-closed for the *new* CLI (nonceMatches rejects a null state), so this is hardening, not an exploit — but the gate reads as covering the flow when it only covers updated clients. Server-side rejection of `mode=cli` without a nonce (after a deprecation window) would close it.

samples.summary: The nonce — now the only thing guarding the loopback callback — is printed to the terminal and travels in a query string, contradicting the doc claim that it "never leaves … and is never persisted"
samples.evidence: `console.error(`Opening browser: ${oauthUrl}`)` (login.ts:47) writes the full URL including `nonce=` to stderr, and the docs explicitly encourage copy-pasting it in headless environments (cli.md line ~176). The same value also rides in the query string of `GET /auth/github`, which nestjs-pino serializes via `url: req.url` (app.module.ts:68) and which any reverse proxy access log records verbatim. docs/design/cli.md's new paragraph asserts "The nonce never leaves the user's machine and the backend except through their own browser, and is never persisted" — shell scrollback, CI job logs, agent transcripts, browser history and proxy logs all falsify that. Attack: anyone who reads one of those within the 30s listener window can POST/GET `http://127.0.0.1:<scanned port>/callback?code=<their code>&state=<leaked nonce>` and log the victim's terminal into the attacker's account, i.e. exactly the attack the nonce was added to stop.

samples.summary: Backend reflects an unauthenticated, attacker-chosen 128-char string into a redirect aimed at an arbitrary loopback port, widening the existing browser-mediated CSRF-to-localhost primitive
samples.evidence: `mode`, `port` and `nonce` on `GET /auth/github` are all unauthenticated attacker-supplied inputs (github-auth.guard.ts:24-26). After the victim completes GitHub consent, auth.controller.ts:130-135 redirects their browser to `http://127.0.0.1:<any 1024-65535>/callback?code=…&state=<attacker string>`. Before this change the query carried only a server-generated random `code`; now up to 128 attacker-chosen characters are reflected into a request the victim's browser makes to an arbitrary local service. `encodeURIComponent` does block CRLF header injection and extra `&`/`=` params, so the payload stays one opaque value — which is why this is minor rather than major — but it is still a one-click reflector into loopback with chosen content. Bounding the nonce to a charset (e.g. /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{16,64}$/) rather than only a length would remove the reflection value.

samples.summary: CLI callback server never checks `req.method`, though the design doc it is being hardened against states it "accepts only GET /callback"
samples.evidence: The request handler at login.ts:187-210 branches only on `url.pathname` and query params; `req.method` is never read. docs/design/cli.md (unchanged context line, ~line 192) claims "The local server binds to `127.0.0.1` only, accepts only `GET /callback`". A cross-origin form POST or any other verb to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=…&state=…` is handled identically. With the new nonce gate this is no longer directly exploitable (the attacker still needs the nonce), which is why it is minor — but the change is precisely the hardening pass where the documented method restriction should have been made real, and the doc now overstates the guard.
searchedFor: grep 'req.method' in packages/cli/src — no hits in login.ts

samples.summary: The `csrf` token that rest-api.md (re-asserted in this diff) says is "embedded in the encoded state" is generated and stored but never embedded or verified anywhere
samples.evidence: `createState` mints `csrf = randomBytes(32)` (cli-auth.store.ts:32) and returns it, but github-auth.guard.ts:31 destructures only `{ stateToken }` and discards it; `consumeState` returns `csrf` (cli-auth.store.ts:57) and auth.controller.ts:120-136 never reads it. Repo-wide grep for `csrf` finds only the store, its spec, and an unrelated cookie comment — there is no comparison site. The diff's rest-api.md hunk restates "The backend generates a CSRF token (random 32 bytes, TTL 5 minutes, in-memory map) and embeds it in the encoded `state`", which the code does not do. In practice the random `stateToken` itself serves the OAuth state/CSRF role, so I do not believe this is exploitable — but it is a documented security control that does not exist, which makes the flow read as more covered than it is.
searchedFor: grep -i csrf across packages/ — only cli-auth.store.ts, its spec, and a cookie comment

finding.summary: CLI auth code is still not bound to the client (no PKCE); the nonce only gates the local listener, so an intercepted code is fully redeemable
finding.evidence: The change cites RFC 8252 §8.9, whose actual prescription for the loopback-redirect code-injection problem is PKCE. What landed is a `state` echo checked only inside the CLI's own listener (`packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:206`). The code itself remains an unbound bearer: `POST /auth/cli/exchange` (auth.controller.ts:152-168) takes `{ code }` with no authentication, no `code_verifier`, and no reference to the nonce — `consumeCode` looks up only the code (cli-auth.store.ts:71). Attack: anyone who observes the code within its 60s TTL — from the victim's browser history/URL bar (`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=…` is a real navigation), a browser extension, a shared/kiosk machine, or an intercepting proxy — POSTs it to /auth/cli/exchange and receives the victim's `accessToken` + `refreshToken`. The nonce does nothing here because the CLI listener is not in the path. Grepped the whole repo for pkce/code_verifier/code_challenge: zero hits. Severity is 'major' rather than 'critical' because it needs code interception, and confidence is low because I could not demonstrate a concrete interception channel in this codebase.

verdict.reason: The absence is real and I could not produce any counterexample. `CliExchangeDto` (auth.dto.ts:3-7) accepts only `code`; `POST /auth/cli/exchange` (auth.controller.ts:152-168) is unguarded (unlike `getMe` at :40-41) and returns access+refresh tokens after `consumeCode(body.code)`. `CodeEntry` (cli-auth.store.ts:17-20) stores only `{userId, expiresAt}` and `consumeCode` (:71-79) keys solely on the code — the CLI nonce lives on `StateEntry` (:13), is consumed at the state step, and is never carried onto the code. The nonce is merely echoed as `&state=` on the loopback redirect (auth.controller.ts:126-135) and checked only inside the CLI's own listener (login.ts:206), so it is bypassed entirely by redeeming the code directly against the server; the CLI's own exchange sends `{ code }` alone (login.ts:66-70). I searched beyond the reviewer's greps: repo-wide for pkce/verifier/challenge/sha256/createHash (hits only in agent scripts, lockfiles, yorkie-signature.guard.ts, api-key.service.ts — none in the CLI auth path), every CliAuthStore/createCode/consumeCode call site, and any indirect loopback/IP binding on the exchange (`req.ip`/`remoteAddress` appear only for rate limiting, main.ts:34, user-throttler.guard.ts:25). No proof-of-possession or client binding exists anywhere. This sits in the crypto/auth lane (weakened auth binding on an unauthenticated token-issuing endpoint) and matches the rubric's `major` band: a clear weakness that requires an interception channel to become a full exploit, so it stays on the gate.

finding.summary: Localhost OAuth callback accepts any `code` with no CLI-generated nonce/state binding (pre-existing, outside the diff) — login-confusion / session fixation
finding.evidence: `startCallbackServer` (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:168-182) serves 127.0.0.1/callback and resolves on the first `code` query param it sees, with no check that the code corresponds to the OAuth flow this process started: no CLI-generated nonce is embedded in the `?mode=cli&port=` URL (line 36) and none is verified on the callback, and there is no Origin/Sec-Fetch check. The code is then exchanged unconditionally at line 56 and the resulting tokens persisted at line 138. Attack: while a victim runs `wafflebase login` (a 30s window, line 237), an attacker who has obtained a valid CLI code for their OWN account gets the victim's browser to issue `GET http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<attacker-code>` (img/fetch; the opaque response does not matter) and races the legitimate callback across the ephemeral port range. If the attacker's code lands first, the victim's CLI session is fixed to the attacker's account and subsequent `files upload` / `docs import` operations write the victim's data into the attacker's workspace. I could not confirm the port-guessing race is practical in the wild, hence low confidence; this code predates the diff and I cite it because the login action has no try/catch and therefore lands in the `runCli` catch this change modified.

verdict.reason: The finding claims the localhost OAuth callback has no CLI-generated nonce/state binding, but the code implements exactly that binding. login.ts:42 mints a 32-byte CSPRNG nonce and passes it to startCallbackServer(nonce) (line 43); login.ts:46 embeds it in the OAuth start URL as &nonce=... (contradicting the claim about "line 36"); login.ts:196-210 does NOT resolve on the first code param -- it returns 400 "Invalid state" unless the callback echoes the nonce back as state, verified constant-time via timingSafeEqual in nonceMatches (login.ts:164-169). callbackResolve(code) at line 253 is only reachable past that gate. The server closes the loop: github-auth.guard.ts:26-37 stores the nonce with the state token and auth.controller.ts:127-135 echoes it as &state= on the 127.0.0.1 redirect, so the gate is live rather than vestigial. The described attack (forged GET /callback?code=attacker-code with no or guessed state) is rejected at line 206 without settling the promise, and the listener deliberately stays open so the genuine callback still arrives; the attacker would need the 256-bit nonce, which never leaves the victim machine except to the configured server. packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts:14-31 asserts no-state -> 400, wrong-state -> 400, matching-state -> 200 with waitForCallback() resolving the real code. The exchange (line 66) and saveSession (line 148) are therefore only reachable with a nonce-bound code, so the code is not present as described.
